Firefighters let home burn over $75 fee -- again

I might be in the minority, but I have no issue with this action.

The city has said very clearly that it doesn't have money and has to supplement the fire department with fees that it charged everyone.

The couple did not pay their part.

To me this is no different than if they didn't have insurance on their stuff. If they didn't, should I blame the insurance company for not paying them for lost product?

Now if they're trapped inside or if there is a pet involved then it shouldn't matter if they paid the fee or not. But the idea that they said "we didn't think this would happen to us" infers that they were aware of the fee and didn't think it necessary.

It's harsh, but I don't consider it unfair.
Agreed. Now they can use all that money they saved on the fee to remodel/replace their home. That's the decisions responsible people make, sometimes you win, sometimes you lose.

"It's the second time in two years firefighters in the area have watched a house burn because of unpaid fees. Last year, Gene Cranick of Obion County and his family lost all of their possessions in a house fire, along with three dogs and a cat, because the fire fee wasn't paid."

And I disagree, this is an essential security service for every community that should not have to be flat out bought like a subscription or fucking mob protection. If the county seriously cannot afford to run the department then they need to look at their budget, cut other shit, or raise the taxes. One families home burning affects the whole community.

This fee is just a different way of paying taxes though. I get that you think it's extortion, but as I said before, if they are still rescuing any life as well as they can, then one refusing to pay taxes/fees should come with the penalties involved.

To me the essential part of a firefighter is saving lives. There is no part of 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' that includes possessions or materials.

Let me ask it from a different perspective. If I don't have renters insurance and my house gets robbed, should the insurance company still pay for me to recover my stuff?

If you don't pay the taxes however they are assessed whether through income tax, property tax or a separate fee (which is probably because they are being serviced by a fire station that is not part of their county, etc.), why should you still be able to reap the benefits of that? Isn't that getting something for nothing?

I do think that if they let a pet die, then something needs to be done. But if a community does not have its own fire department as it is outside the city limits, then the idea that them refusing to pay the fee for the extra costs incurred to travel to rural county areas should come with a risk that is taken by the homeowner. If something happens, then the blame is not on the firefighters but on the people unwilling to pay the costs.

If it's a matter of costs too, then perhaps a credit could be given to those whose incomes are below poverty level.

I read that satellites need propulsion to stay in orbit and not fall on earth. But how are they refueled? I never heard of that!
as far as I know they generally don't get refueled. the amount of fuel required to stop orbit decay isn't insurmountable, but it does mean satellites have a limited shelf life.

Most are never refueled and their orbit slowly decays and they ride down into the atmosphere.

Some are refuelable (a handful?), most notable, the Hubble Space Telescope. It is extremely expensive to send a manned mission to handle the refueling and I don't recall ever hearing of any method of robotic refueling, though it is certainly possible. There have been many automated docking procedures in the past.

They don't need a lot of fuel... they just send them up with some fuel. If there was no air or debris or anything, they would just circle the earth forever. They just need a tiny spurt of propulsion every now and then to compensate for being slowed down by the bit of air or whatever that is up there. When they are orbiting, the earth is pulling them towards earth with nearly the same force as on the surface (sometimes people think there is no gravity in earth orbit, but it only feels that way), but they are moving sideways so fast that they end up going in a circle (they'd go in a straight line if earth didn't keep pulling them toward it!). But as they plow through air or dust or whatever crap is up there, they slow down, and then earth pulls them down faster than they can go sideways, and as they get lower they hit even more air, slow down even more, and eventually burn up in the atmosphere, if they aren't boosted again.

They can get power from the sun, or nuclear power, but right now rockets have to have some sort of mass that they can shoot out in the opposite direction that they want to go, so they are limited by that. What's interesting is that some people are working on a system that can produce thrust without mass (reactionless drive)... right now it supposedly produces only a tiny amount of thrust, and skeptics wonder if there is just a mistake in the measurements, but it'd be quite interesting if they could do that. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RF_resonant_cavity_thruster
Producing thrust without expelling any mass? Forgive me if I'm wrong but wouldn't that go against Newton's 3rd law of motion?
The propellers spin and in doing so push air backwards, thus pushing the plane forwards.
Mass isn't lost, but it is expelled backwards by the propeller.
All aircraft take air and accelerate it in order to derive thrust.
I understand that, but there's no loss in mass with a solar powered aircraft, which is what the guy I replied to said is necessary.

Yes, yes it does. No one really knows why it works but it's been tested a few times now and the conservation of momentum seems to be violated consistently. It's weird, and maybe we'll find out someday.

Maybe I'm misreading this, but orbit doesn't require thrust. Essentially, an object in orbit is falling to earth constantly but it "missses," and gravity keeps it from leaving in a straight line. So it's just Newton's 3rd plus gravity that keeps it in orbit.

Not in theory but in reality, there are several factors that can cause orbits to decay (lose velocity until it crashes). For things in earth orbit, especially LEO, the atmosphere is the big one. There's obviously near-0 air resistance 100km up, but it's nonzero, so constantly slamming into the rarified atmosphere up there slows the satellite down until it doesn't have enough lateral velocity to miss the Earth any longer. Attaching a small rocket engine (or ion thruster) and firing it periodically can boost the satellite so it stays in orbit longer.
